title: Stratified Analysis – Mantel–Haenszel, Effect Modification and Simpson’s Paradox

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Stratified analysis splits the data into strata (layers) defined by a third variable, computes the exposure–outcome measure within each stratum, and, if the stratum measures agree, combines them into one adjusted estimate. The Mantel–Haenszel (MH) estimators (Mantel & Haenszel, 1959) are weighted averages of the stratum-specific measures. For stratum i with the 2 × 2 layout of §10.6.4 (aᵢ = exposed with outcome, bᵢ = exposed without, cᵢ = unexposed with, dᵢ = unexposed without, nᵢ = stratum total):

OR_MH = Σ(aᵢdᵢ/nᵢ) ÷ Σ(bᵢcᵢ/nᵢ)

RR_MH = Σ[aᵢ(cᵢ + dᵢ)/nᵢ] ÷ Σ[cᵢ(aᵢ + bᵢ)/nᵢ]

Effect modification is present when the true exposure effect differs between strata. Simpson’s paradox is the extreme case of confounding in which the crude association points the opposite way to the association in every stratum.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Stratification is the simplest way to compare like with like. If the third variable is a confounder, then within each of its strata it cannot confound, because it does not vary there. You compute the risk ratio separately in each stratum, check that the stratum answers agree, and pool them.

The stratified analysis answers two separate questions:

  1. Do the stratum-specific measures differ from each other? If yes, beyond what chance would produce, the third variable is an effect modifier. Report the stratum-specific estimates; a single pooled number would hide the finding.
  2. If they agree, does the pooled (MH) estimate differ from the crude one? If yes, the third variable was confounding the crude estimate. Report the MH estimate.

The two questions are distinct, not opposite. A variable can be a confounder, an effect modifier, both, or neither. Confounding is a distortion of the crude estimate, and you remove it. Effect modification is a real feature of the effect, and you report it.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why the MH OR is an average of the stratum ORs. Write ORᵢ = aᵢdᵢ/(bᵢcᵢ) and choose weights wᵢ = bᵢcᵢ/nᵢ. Then:

  1. wᵢ × ORᵢ = (bᵢcᵢ/nᵢ) × aᵢdᵢ/(bᵢcᵢ) = aᵢdᵢ/nᵢ.
  2. Weighted average = Σwᵢ ORᵢ ÷ Σwᵢ = Σ(aᵢdᵢ/nᵢ) ÷ Σ(bᵢcᵢ/nᵢ) = OR_MH.
  3. The weights are larger for bigger, more balanced strata, and a stratum with a zero cell still contributes, which a simple average of the ORs cannot do.

The same algebra with wᵢ = cᵢ(aᵢ + bᵢ)/nᵢ gives RR_MH as a weighted average of the stratum RRs.

The MH chi-square test. Under H₀ (no association in any stratum), and with the margins of each table fixed, aᵢ has expected value E(aᵢ) = (aᵢ + bᵢ)(aᵢ + cᵢ)/nᵢ and variance V(aᵢ) = (aᵢ + bᵢ)(cᵢ + dᵢ)(aᵢ + cᵢ)(bᵢ + dᵢ) ÷ [nᵢ²(nᵢ − 1)]. Summing over strata:

χ²_MH = [Σaᵢ − ΣE(aᵢ)]² ÷ ΣV(aᵢ), on 1 degree of freedom.

It asks whether the exposed have more outcomes than expected, pooling the evidence from all strata.

A test of homogeneity. Woolf’s method (Woolf, 1955) weights each stratum’s log RR (or log OR) by the inverse of its variance, wᵢ = 1/SE²(ln RRᵢ), with SE²(ln RR) = 1/a − 1/(a + b) + 1/c − 1/(c + d) (recall §10.6.4). Then

Q = Σwᵢ(ln RRᵢ − ln RR_w)², where ln RR_w = Σwᵢ ln RRᵢ ÷ Σwᵢ,

is compared with χ² on (number of strata − 1) df. The Breslow–Day test (Breslow & Day, 1980) is an alternative for odds ratios. Both can have low power when strata are small, so a non-significant result is weak evidence that the effects are the same.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Recall the cohort of 200 infants in §8.7 and §10.6.4: not exclusively breastfed (not EBF) versus EBF, followed for diarrhoea. Crude RR = 3.54 (95% CI 2.02 to 6.17); crude OR = 5.32. The infants came from two PHCs:

Stratum Exposure Diarrhoea No diarrhoea Total Risk
PHC Urban Not EBF 9 21 30 0.300
EBF 9 81 90 0.100
PHC Rural Not EBF 24 26 50 0.480
EBF 5 25 30 0.167
Both (crude) Not EBF 33 47 80 0.413
EBF 14 106 120 0.117

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Stratum RRs: urban 0.300 ÷ 0.100 = 3.00; rural 0.480 ÷ 0.167 = 2.88. Stratum ORs: urban (9 × 81)/(21 × 9) = 3.86; rural (24 × 25)/(26 × 5) = 4.62.
  2. Homogeneity (Woolf, RR). Urban: SE² = 1/9 − 1/30 + 1/9 − 1/90 = 0.178, w = 5.63, ln RR = 1.099. Rural: SE² = 1/24 − 1/50 + 1/5 − 1/30 = 0.188, w = 5.31, ln RR = 1.058. Pooled ln RR_w = 1.079. Q = 5.63(0.020)² + 5.31(0.021)² = 0.005 on 1 df, p = 0.95. No evidence of effect modification on the RR scale. (For the ORs, the Breslow–Day test gives χ² = 0.054, p = 0.82.)
  3. MH RR: numerator 9 × 90/120 + 24 × 30/80 = 6.75 + 9.00 = 15.75; denominator 9 × 30/120 + 5 × 50/80 = 2.25 + 3.125 = 5.375. RR_MH = 15.75 ÷ 5.375 = 2.93. Its 95% CI, 1.60 to 5.35, uses the Mantel–Haenszel variance formula for the RR, which is long by hand and usually left to software.
  4. MH OR: numerator 9 × 81/120 + 24 × 25/80 = 6.075 + 7.500 = 13.575; denominator 21 × 9/120 + 26 × 5/80 = 1.575 + 1.625 = 3.200. OR_MH = 13.575 ÷ 3.200 = 4.24.
  5. MH χ²: E(a) = 30 × 18/120 = 4.50 (urban) and 50 × 29/80 = 18.125 (rural), total 22.625, against 33 observed. V = 2.893 + 4.388 = 7.281. χ²_MH = (33 − 22.625)² ÷ 7.281 = 107.64 ÷ 7.281 = 14.78, p = 0.0001.
  6. Crude versus adjusted: 3.54 against 2.93, a ratio of 1.21. PHC was confounding: not-EBF infants were concentrated in the rural PHC (50 of 80 rural infants, 62.5%, against 30 of 120 urban, 25%), and diarrhoea was commoner there even among EBF infants (16.7% against 10.0%). Part of the crude excess was the rural PHC, not feeding.

Conclusion: after allowing for PHC, not being exclusively breastfed is associated with about three times the risk of diarrhoea (RR_MH 2.93, 95% CI 1.60 to 5.35), and the association is similar in both PHCs.

Whether a crude-versus-adjusted gap of this size “matters” is a judgement. Comparing the change in estimate against a pre-stated size is one way to decide which confounders to keep; in simulations it tended to do better than significance testing when the right decision was not obvious (Mickey & Greenland, 1989). The decision to treat PHC as a potential confounder, however, comes from the causal reasoning of §11.6.1, not from the size of the change.

Simpson’s paradox with numbers. An illustrative example (hypothetical counts). Two PHCs treat children admitted with diarrhoea; the outcome is treatment failure (referral onwards). PHC A has an inpatient ward and receives most of the severely dehydrated children.

Severity PHC Failures Children Risk
Severe A 12 100 0.120
B 3 20 0.150
Not severe A 1 50 0.020
B 6 200 0.030
Both (crude) A 13 150 0.087
B 9 220 0.041
  1. Within each severity stratum PHC A does better: RR (A vs B) = 0.12 ÷ 0.15 = 0.80 for severe, 0.02 ÷ 0.03 = 0.67 for non-severe.
  2. Crude, PHC A looks worse: RR = 0.087 ÷ 0.041 = 2.12.
  3. The reason: two-thirds of A’s children (100 of 150) were severe, against one-eleventh of B’s (20 of 220). Severity is a cause of failure and is associated with the PHC. It confounds the crude comparison strongly enough to reverse it.
  4. RR_MH = (12 × 20/120 + 1 × 200/250) ÷ (3 × 100/120 + 6 × 50/250) = (2.0 + 0.8) ÷ (2.5 + 1.2) = 2.8 ÷ 3.7 = 0.76. Adjusted for severity, A’s failure risk is about three-quarters of B’s.

The same reversal appeared with district death rates in §7.4.2, where age played the part of severity.

blocks.caption: Figure 11.5. Left: diarrhoea risk by feeding within each PHC and crude (canonical cohort); the stratum RRs (3.00, 2.88) agree with each other and are lower than the crude 3.54: confounding. Right: the illustrative Simpson’s paradox table; PHC A has the lower risk in each severity stratum but the higher crude risk.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
eb <- read.csv("data/ebf_diarrhoea_cohort.csv")
tab <- table(exposure  = factor(eb$not_ebf, levels = c(1, 0),
                                labels = c("Not EBF", "EBF")),
             diarrhoea = factor(eb$diarrhoea, levels = c(1, 0),
                                labels = c("Yes", "No")),
             phc       = eb$phc)
mantelhaen.test(tab, correct = FALSE)
library(epiR)
epi.2by2(tab, method = "cohort.count")
    Mantel-Haenszel chi-squared test without continuity correction

The table is built with “Not EBF” and “Yes” first so that cell a is exposed-with-outcome, as in §10.6.4. mantelhaen.test gives χ²_MH = 14.78 (step 5) and OR_MH = 4.24 (step 4) with its CI. epi.2by2 adds the crude and MH risk ratios (3.54 and 2.93, step 3), their ratio 1.21 (step 6), and the homogeneity test of the RRs (χ² = 0.005, p = 0.95, step 2). By default mantelhaen.test applies a continuity correction; correct = FALSE matches the hand calculation. The OR homogeneity line (χ² = 0.027) is not the Breslow–Day test of step 2 (0.054): epi.2by2 uses Woolf’s method on the log ORs after adding 0.5 to every cell. Both find no evidence that the ORs differ.

points.html: Decision rule. First test homogeneity. If the stratum estimates clearly differ, report them separately (effect modification). If they agree, compare crude and MH: a material difference means confounding, so report the MH estimate; little difference means the variable did not confound, and the crude estimate may be reported.
Interaction and confounding are distinct, not opposite. PHC in the cohort confounded (3.54 vs 2.93) without modifying (3.00 vs 2.88).

Effect modification depends on the scale. The same cohort shows almost equal RRs (3.00, 2.88) but different risk differences (0.20 urban, 0.31 rural). Say which measure you mean, and give the stratum-specific RRs, ORs or RDs so readers can judge (Knol & VanderWeele, 2012).

Stratification works for one or two categorical confounders. With several, strata multiply and empty out; a continuous confounder must be cut into categories, which leaves residual confounding within the categories (Tripepi et al., 2010). Regression (Chapters 12–13) adjusts for many variables at once.
With matched pairs as strata, the MH OR equals the matched-pair OR b/c (recall §10.8): for the 80 pairs in matched_casecontrol.csv both give 2.4.
The MH OR is valid for case-control data (it uses only odds); the MH RR needs cohort or cross-sectional data, where risks can be estimated (recall §10.6.4).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 11.3

questions.prompt: Two strata of a cohort give (a, b, c, d) = (10, 20, 5, 40) and (15, 10, 20, 30), with 75 people in each. Compute the stratum ORs, the crude OR and OR_MH. Did the stratifying variable confound the crude OR, and in which direction?
questions.answer:
1. Stratum 1: OR = (10 × 40) ÷ (20 × 5) = 400 ÷ 100 = 4.00. Stratum 2: OR = (15 × 30) ÷ (10 × 20) = 450 ÷ 200 = 2.25.
  2. Crude table: a = 25, b = 30, c = 25, d = 70. Crude OR = (25 × 70) ÷ (30 × 25) = 1,750 ÷ 750 = 2.33.
  3. OR_MH: numerator 10 × 40/75 + 15 × 30/75 = 5.333 + 6.000 = 11.333; denominator 20 × 5/75 + 10 × 20/75 = 1.333 + 2.667 = 4.000. OR_MH = 11.333 ÷ 4.000 = 2.83.
  4. The adjusted OR (2.83) is larger than the crude (2.33): the stratifying variable confounded the crude estimate towards the null (negative confounding). (MH χ² = 7.55, p = 0.006.) Before pooling, check that 4.00 and 2.25 are compatible with one common OR; with strata of 75 the homogeneity test has little power.

questions.prompt: In a study of tobacco chewing and oral leukoplakia, the RR is 1.2 among non-drinkers and 4.5 among drinkers; the homogeneity test gives p = 0.002. What should the authors report, and why is an MH RR inappropriate?
questions.answer: Drinking is an effect modifier: the RRs differ far more than chance would explain. The authors should report the two stratum-specific RRs (with CIs), and say that the association with tobacco chewing is much stronger among drinkers. An MH RR is a weighted average that assumes one common RR; here it would describe neither group and hide the main finding.

questions.prompt: In the illustrative Simpson’s paradox table of §11.7, apply PHC A’s severity-specific failure risks to PHC B’s mix of children (20 severe, 200 not severe). What overall failure risk would A have had? Compare it with B’s crude risk and explain the paradox in one sentence.
questions.answer:
1. Expected failures at A with B’s mix: 20 × 0.12 + 200 × 0.02 = 2.4 + 4.0 = 6.4.
  2. Risk = 6.4 ÷ 220 = 0.029 (2.9%), against B’s actual 9 ÷ 220 = 0.041 (4.1%).

With the same case mix, A does better than B; A’s crude risk is higher only because two-thirds of its children were severely dehydrated, and severity, not the PHC, drives most failures. (This is direct standardisation, recall §7.4.2, with B’s case mix as the standard.)
